The best AI coding assistants in 2026 are Claude Code for terminal-first agentic work, GitHub Copilot for teams that live in GitHub, Cursor for an AI-first editor, OpenAI Codex CLI for teams already paying for ChatGPT, Devin Desktop (the former Windsurf) for running fleets of agents, and Cline for bring-your-own-model control. Entry prices run from $0 to $20 a month, but the real cost depends on usage quotas, which every vendor on this list changed at least once in 2026.
Last verified: October 2026

These tools come in three shapes: IDE extensions (Copilot, Cline), AI-first editors (Cursor, Devin Desktop), and terminal-first coding agents (Claude Code, Codex CLI). Picking the wrong shape for how your team works costs more than picking the wrong vendor within a shape. This guide compares all six on pricing taken from each vendor's own pricing page and features checked against their own documentation on October 21, 2026.

Disclosure: this guide does not cite G2 or Capterra star ratings. Review-aggregator pages for this category are heavily bot-gated, and a rating we cannot confirm directly is not something we present as verified. Two of the six tools changed hands or names this year (Cursor and Windsurf), and both changes are called out in their entries.
How we compared these tools

We asked three questions, in order. (1) What shape is it? An extension that suggests code inside an editor you already use is a different product from an agent that plans, edits across a repo, and runs commands on its own. (2) What does it cost to run? Some tools bundle model access into a flat subscription, some charge per seat with a pool of usage credits, and some are free but require you to bring your own API key and pay the model provider directly. (3) Who builds it, and who owns it? Whether an assistant is a first-party model-lab product, an editor owned by a company with its own model to promote, or a free open-source client changes how much you can trust its roadmap and model choice to stay stable.

Best AI coding assistants: quick overview
If you want a terminal-first agent that plans, edits, tests, and commits across a whole repo: start with Claude Code, Anthropic's own agent, included in every paid Claude plan.
If your team already lives inside GitHub and VS Code: start with GitHub Copilot for the broadest editor support and native pull request workflows.
If you want an AI-first editor with built-in agents: consider Cursor, keeping in mind that its cheapest paid plan is now limited to Grok models.
If your team already pays for ChatGPT: consider OpenAI Codex CLI, which is included in every ChatGPT plan from Free upward.
If you want to manage many local and cloud agents from one desktop app: consider Devin Desktop from Cognition, the product Windsurf became.
If you want full control over which model powers your agent: consider Cline, free and open source, bring your own API key.

1. Claude Code, best for a terminal-first agent with deep multi-file reasoning

Claude Code is Anthropic's agentic coding tool: it plans a task, edits across an entire repository, runs tests and commands, and commits, working from the terminal or from its VS Code, JetBrains, desktop, and web surfaces. It is extended through CLAUDE.md project instructions, skills, hooks, subagents, and MCP servers, according to Anthropic's Claude Code documentation, and it runs on Anthropic's current Claude 5 family (Fable 5.1, Opus 5.5, Sonnet 5.5, and Haiku 5.5, as listed on claude.com/pricing in October 2026).
Best for: engineers comfortable in a terminal who want an agent that reasons across a whole codebase and can be extended with custom skills and hooks, not a completion popup inside an editor.

Pricing (confirmed on claude.com/pricing, October 21, 2026): Claude Code is included in paid Claude plans, not sold separately, and the Free plan does not include it. Pro is $20/month, or $17/month billed annually ($200 up front). Max starts at $100/month, with 5x or 20x the usage of Pro. Team Standard seats are $25/seat/month ($20 billed annually) and Premium seats are $125/seat/month ($100 billed annually), for teams of 2 to 150. Enterprise starts at $20/seat/month billed annually with a 20-seat minimum, plus usage at API rates. You can also run it on pay-as-you-go API billing; Sonnet 5.5 lists at $2 per million input tokens and $10 per million output tokens.

Pros: whole-repo reasoning with a git-native plan, edit, test, commit loop; the deepest extension surface of the six (skills, hooks, subagents, MCP); first-party product from the lab that trains the model.

Cons: the terminal-first workflow has a learning curve for developers used to an IDE assistant; Pro-tier usage limits run out quickly on large repos, which pushes heavy daily users to Max or Premium seats; you are tied to Claude models unless you configure a third-party provider.
For a head-to-head on the two most common shortlist pairings, see our GitHub Copilot vs Claude Code comparison.
2. GitHub Copilot, best for teams already living in GitHub and VS Code

GitHub Copilot has the broadest editor footprint on this list, with support for VS Code, Visual Studio, JetBrains IDEs, Eclipse, Vim/Neovim, and Xcode according to GitHub's own feature matrix, plus Copilot CLI and a cloud agent that works on issues and opens pull requests inside GitHub. It is the lowest-friction rollout for a team whose whole software lifecycle already runs on GitHub.
Best for: teams standardized on GitHub that want an assistant they can roll out without switching editors or workflows.

Pricing (confirmed on github.com/features/copilot/plans and GitHub Docs, October 21, 2026): Free is $0 with limited chat and agent usage; Pro is $10/month; Pro+ is $39/month; Max is $100/month; Business is $19 per granted seat per month; Enterprise is $39 per granted seat per month. Usage is now measured in GitHub AI Credits (1 credit = $0.01), and agent mode, code review, the cloud agent, and Copilot CLI consume credits, while code completions and next edit suggestions do not. From June 1, 2026, code review workflows also consume GitHub Actions minutes.
Pros: the widest editor support of any tool here; native integration with GitHub pull requests, issues, and Actions; a real free tier, plus free access for verified students.

Cons: credit-based billing makes monthly cost harder to predict for heavy agent users; GitHub may use interactions from Free, Pro, and Pro+ users for model training unless they opt out, which matters for teams using personal plans.
3. Cursor, best for an AI-first editor with built-in agents

Cursor is an AI-first code editor built around its Agent, with cloud agents and automations, Bugbot AI code review, and team rules, skills, and plugins on higher tiers. In June 2026 SpaceX agreed to acquire Anysphere, Cursor's maker, in a stock deal valued at about $60 billion, and Cursor's plans now center on xAI's Grok models.

Best for: developers who want an editor designed around agent workflows rather than an extension added to an existing editor, and who are comfortable with Grok as the default model or willing to pay API rates for others.

Pricing (confirmed on cursor.com/pricing, October 21, 2026): Free is $0 with limited Agent and Chat requests; Plus is $8/month and only Grok models are available on it; Premium is $30/month and adds cloud agents, Bugbot code reviews, and third-party models billed at API list price; Super is $100/month; Ultra is $200/month; Teams starts at $30/user/month; Enterprise is custom. Usage allowances refresh weekly, and Premium and higher do not include an allowance for third-party models, so Claude or GPT usage is billed on top.
Pros: an editor built around agents from the ground up; cloud agents that keep working after you close the laptop; a low $8 entry point if Grok fits your work.

Cons: using Claude, GPT, or Gemini models now means Premium or higher plus separate usage billing, which changes the cost math for teams that chose Cursor for multi-model access; the ownership change is recent, so the roadmap may keep shifting.
If you are choosing between editors and agents, our Windsurf vs Cursor vs Claude Code breakdown goes deeper on workflow fit.
4. OpenAI Codex CLI, best for teams already paying for ChatGPT

OpenAI Codex CLI is an open-source terminal coding agent ("lightweight coding agent that runs in your terminal," per its GitHub repository, Apache 2.0 license) that uses your ChatGPT plan instead of a separate subscription. Codex also runs in an IDE extension, on the web, in a desktop app, and on iOS, and all of them share one usage pool with ChatGPT.
Best for: individuals or teams already paying for ChatGPT who want an agentic coding CLI without adding a second AI subscription.

Pricing (confirmed on OpenAI's Codex pricing documentation, October 21, 2026): the CLI is free and open source. Codex is included in ChatGPT Free ($0) and Go ($8/month) for lightweight tasks; Plus ($20/month) adds Codex on the web, CLI, IDE extension, and iOS with GPT-6.1 Sol and GPT-6 Luna; Pro comes in $100, $200, and $500/month tiers; Business is $20/user/month billed annually ($25 monthly, 2+ users); Enterprise and Edu are contact-sales. You can also sign in with an API key and pay API rates, which skips the cloud features such as GitHub code review and Slack.
Pros: no extra license cost if you already have ChatGPT; open source, so the client is auditable; an API-key mode that suits CI pipelines.

Cons: limits are governed by your ChatGPT plan and shared with regular ChatGPT use, so heavy chat users eat into coding capacity; OpenAI retires models from Codex on a schedule (GPT-5.5 left Codex for ChatGPT sign-in on October 14, 2026), so workflows tied to one model need upkeep. If you want Codex agents wired into CI with review gates, our Codex development agency builds that setup.
5. Devin Desktop (formerly Windsurf), best for managing fleets of coding agents

Devin Desktop is Cognition's desktop app for running and managing local and cloud coding agents with a full IDE built in, and it is the product the Windsurf editor became: windsurf.com and windsurf.com/pricing now permanently redirect to devin.ai. Cognition, the company behind the Devin autonomous engineer, acquired Windsurf in 2025, and the Pro plan now bundles access to Devin Cloud agents and Cognition's SWE-2 model.
Best for: teams that want one surface to plan, delegate, review, and ship work across several agents at once, and who are comfortable re-checking plan terms as the product keeps evolving.

Pricing (confirmed on devin.ai/pricing, October 21, 2026): Free is $0 with a light agent quota and unlimited Tab completions; Pro is $20/month with frontier models from OpenAI, Anthropic, Google, and SpaceXAI, free SWE-2 use, and Devin Cloud access; Max is $200/month with significantly higher quotas; Teams is $80/month for the team plan plus $40/month per full developer seat, up to 200 users; Enterprise is custom. Quotas refresh daily and weekly, and extra usage is billed at API pricing.
Pros: built for running several agents in parallel, not one chat at a time; cloud agents included from the $20 Pro tier; multi-provider model access on paid plans.
Cons: the Windsurf brand, pricing, and billing model have changed several times since the acquisition, so any number here needs re-checking at purchase; the desktop download currently targets macOS.

6. Cline, best for full control over which model powers your agent

Cline is a free, open-source coding agent that runs as an extension in VS Code, Cursor, JetBrains, and Windsurf, as a CLI, and as a desktop app, built around bring-your-own-API-key rather than a flat subscription. Per Cline's pricing page, the open-source agent is completely free for individual developers, and you pay only for model inference, with no markup.
Best for: developers or teams who want to choose exactly which model powers their agent and would rather pay a model provider directly than pay a subscription with usage caps.

Pricing (confirmed on cline.bot/pricing and Cline's documentation, October 21, 2026): free for individual developers, paying only for inference with your own keys; an optional ClinePass subscription at $9.99/month gives 2 to 5x the usage on curated open coding models compared with standard API rates; Enterprise is custom-priced and adds SSO, an SLA, centralized billing, and dedicated support.

Pros: no subscription markup on model usage; works with any compatible provider, so you are not locked into one lab's roadmap; open source and auditable; Plan and Act modes, skills, hooks, and MCP support.
Cons: no bundled frontier-model access, so you manage API spend as a separate line item; setup takes more steps than a one-click subscription.
How to choose the best AI coding assistant for your team
1) Editor extension, AI-first editor, or terminal agent?
Start from where your engineers already work, not from a feature list.
If your team will not switch editors: GitHub Copilot or Cline, both of which run inside the IDE you already have.
If you are willing to adopt a new editor built around agents: Cursor or Devin Desktop.
If your senior engineers live in the terminal and want an agent to own whole tasks: Claude Code or Codex CLI.
2) Subscription, per-seat credits, or bring your own key?

The sticker price is the least useful number on these pricing pages. Claude Code, Codex, and Devin Desktop bundle usage into a plan with quotas; Copilot and Cursor meter agent work through credits or weekly allowances; Cline passes model cost straight through.
If you want a predictable monthly bill per developer: a Claude Team seat, a ChatGPT Business seat, or a Devin Desktop Teams seat.
If you want to pay exactly for what you use: Cline with your own keys, or Codex and Claude Code on API billing.
Run a two-week pilot on a real repo and read the usage dashboard before committing to annual seats.
3) Which models do you need?

Model access is now the biggest hidden variable. Cursor's $8 Plus plan is Grok-only, Claude Code runs on Claude models, Codex on OpenAI models, and Cline and Devin Desktop let you mix providers. If your team has already standardized on one model family for quality or compliance reasons, that narrows the list fast.
4) Who owns the rollout?

Every tool here gets better with shared project rules, instructions files, and guardrails on what the agent can run. A team that installs an agent without those usually gets inconsistent output and a security review it was not ready for. Budget time for setup, not only licenses.

Red flags when evaluating an AI coding assistant

A vendor page that will not state a price without a sales call, in a category where most competitors publish clear tiers. Ask what a comparable team-size deployment costs before you sit through a demo.
"Full autonomy" marketing with no word on what happens when the agent gets something wrong on a production repo.
No visibility into which model powers the tool, and no way to choose or swap it. Cursor's 2026 shift toward Grok shows how quickly a default model can change.
A star rating cited from a review site without a date or a link to the live listing.
Pricing or plan names that changed more than once in six months with no changelog. Windsurf's path to Devin Desktop is the clearest example in this comparison.
FAQ
What is the best AI coding assistant in 2026?

Claude Code is the strongest pick for teams that want an agent to own whole multi-file tasks, while GitHub Copilot is the easiest to roll out for teams already on GitHub. The right answer depends on shape: Copilot and Cline fit inside your existing editor, Cursor and Devin Desktop replace it, and Claude Code and Codex CLI work from the terminal. For no-code and prompt-to-app builders, see our separate guide to the best vibe coding tools.
What is the difference between an AI coding assistant and an AI coding agent?

An assistant suggests code inline as you type, while an agent plans a multi-step task, edits several files, runs tests or builds, and reports back largely on its own. All six tools here now include agent modes, but Claude Code, Codex CLI, and Devin Desktop are built agent-first, while Copilot started as autocomplete and added agents later.
Which AI coding assistant is cheapest?

Cline and OpenAI Codex CLI are free as tools: Cline costs whatever you pay your model provider, and Codex is included in ChatGPT Free, with more capacity from the $8/month Go plan. Among paid subscriptions, Cursor Plus at $8/month is the lowest entry price but only covers Grok models, and GitHub Copilot Pro at $10/month is the cheapest paid plan with a choice of models.
Do I need a paid plan to use Claude Code or OpenAI Codex CLI?

Claude Code needs a paid Claude plan (Pro at $20/month or higher) or API billing, because the Free plan does not include it. Codex works on every ChatGPT plan including Free, but serious daily use needs Plus at $20/month or higher, or an API key with metered billing.
What happened to Windsurf?

Windsurf is now Devin Desktop, Cognition's desktop app for running local and cloud coding agents, and windsurf.com redirects to devin.ai. Pricing on devin.ai in October 2026 is Free, Pro at $20/month, Max at $200/month, and Teams at $80/month plus $40 per full developer seat.
Can I use more than one of these tools at the same time?

Yes, and many developers do, for example running GitHub Copilot for inline completions in VS Code while using Claude Code or Codex CLI in a terminal for larger tasks. The costs stack across subscriptions, so decide which tool owns which job before your team pays for three overlapping plans.
